summary: Mission Control: Build to Launch is a free 3D browser game that teaches the connected decisions behind satellite mission design. Players accept contracts inspired by Landsat, Hubble and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, assemble a spacecraft, choose a rocket and orbit, and aim to return useful science within budget. Live indicators connect mass, electricity, data transmission, cost and engineering margins. A Mission Forecast tablet helps players compare solar storms, station interference, clouds and extended lunar eclipses, including combined effects and equipment protection. After launch, explanations and redesign encourage learning through iteration. Three difficulty levels, a tutorial and Free Mode support different experience levels. NASA mission-design resources and real missions provide educational context; equipment values and event probabilities are simplified gameplay models. Created by Hell0 World! in Buenos Aires for the Space Mission Design Game challenge.
details:
Mission Control: Build to Launch

WHAT IT DOES

A free, single-player 3D browser game about designing satellite missions. Players operate from a space center, accept a contract, assemble a satellite in the hangar, select its rocket and orbit, review the equipment list, and launch. Landsat: Earth Watch explores forests and ice; Hubble: Deep Field explores distant galaxies; LRO: Lunar Mapping explores the lunar south pole. Successful campaign missions unlock the next contract.

HOW IT WORKS

Instruments, solar panels, batteries, antennas and ground stations compete for mass, power and money. Live indicators show mass, power, data, cost, science and risk. The Mission Forecast tablet compares event probabilities, equipment protection and potential science outcomes. Solar storms, ground station interference, cloud cover and extended lunar eclipses can occur together. Players weigh resilience against cost and performance. Meeting the campaign science goal earns an efficiency bonus for unused budget.

Players review the equipment list before launch, time first-stage separation or leave it to the flight computer, then read an explanation of what worked and what to change. Redesign and the Mission Archive support repeated experiments. Cadet, Engineer and Flight Director offer increasing constraints; Free Mode opens every contract without a budget limit while retaining mass, power and mission restrictions.

HOW TO PLAY

Open the public itch.io link in a desktop browser with mouse and keyboard, click Run game, and use fullscreen. The interface is in English. Click to select, hover for descriptions, drag outside the interface to rotate the hangar camera, and use the wheel to zoom. Esc opens the menu, Space separates the first stage, and Enter skips launch. Start with Cadet and the tutorial. Progress, designs, history, settings and rankings are local to the browser; clearing site data may erase them. Free flights do not unlock campaign missions or earn campaign ranking scores.

EDUCATIONAL IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

The game turns linked engineering tradeoffs into visible consequences. A more capable camera only helps when the spacecraft can power it and return its data. Forecasts, simultaneous hazards and post-flight explanations let players compare choices and learn from failure. NASA mission design guidance, the Goddard Mission Design Lab, CubeSat 101 and real mission resources inform the educational content. The goal is accessible systems thinking, not operational mission prediction. Equipment statistics, probabilities and effects are simplified gameplay models. The storm power interruption is an abstraction; the cited Starlink loss involved atmospheric drag.

DEVELOPMENT AND ATTRIBUTION

Created by Hell0 World!, Buenos Aires, with Unity 6.6, C#, Universal Render Pipeline, uGUI and the Input System; distributed as WebGL. Kenney supplies models and particles (CC0), Solar System Scope supplies planet and sky textures (CC BY 4.0), and Chakra Petch and Share Tech Mono use SIL Open Font Licenses. Music and effects are synthesized by code.

AI ASSISTANCE

Claude/Claude Code assisted with research, design, C# code, scene construction and English text. ChatGPT assisted with documentation, presentation and publication configuration. The team defined the game, made design decisions, reviewed changes and tested it. Models, textures and fonts are credited third-party assets; no AI-generated images or video are used. Sound is synthesized by code written with AI assistance.
